flashcards.q: What class of bug does E2E testing catch that integration tests structurally cannot?
flashcards.a: Seam bugs in the actual deployed wiring -- a frontend build silently calling the wrong API version, a broken redirect after login, or a race condition that only appears under real network latency between genuinely deployed services.

flashcards.q: Why were Selenium-era E2E suites notoriously flaky?
flashcards.a: No built-in auto-waiting -- every async interaction needed a hand-written explicit wait, and getting one wrong either raced the page (intermittent failure) or over-waited (slow suite). This, plus manual driver-binary version management and no native parallelism, was the primary historical source of E2E flakiness.

flashcards.q: What does Playwright's auto-waiting locator actually do?
flashcards.a: It retries an action automatically until the target element exists, is visible, is stable (not animating), and is enabled -- removing the need for manual sleep()/explicit-wait boilerplate that plagued Selenium suites.

flashcards.q: What is Playwright's storageState and why does it matter beyond saving time?
flashcards.a: It captures authenticated session state (cookies, local storage) once so tests start already logged in instead of driving the full UI login flow per test. It removes login -- itself a multi-step async flow -- as a shared flakiness source across every test that isn't specifically testing login.

flashcards.q: What locator strategy order minimizes E2E maintenance cost, and why do raw CSS/XPath selectors cause the most breakage?
flashcards.a: Preference order: get_by_role > get_by_label/get_by_text > get_by_test_id > raw CSS/XPath. CSS/XPath ties the test to markup structure, so unrelated visual/structural refactors break tests with zero behavioral change -- the largest source of untraceable E2E maintenance tickets.

flashcards.q: Roughly how many E2E specs before a suite typically becomes a flakiness/maintenance tax rather than a confidence source?
flashcards.a: Roughly 10-50 specs depending on product size -- past that, shared test data and environment issues tend to compound faster than triage discipline keeps up. It's a symptom threshold, not a hard rule; the real test is whether each spec covers a genuinely business-critical, cross-system journey.

flashcards.q: What is the single most common cause of 'flaky in CI, fine locally' E2E failures?
flashcards.a: Shared or polluted test data under parallel execution -- CI runs specs concurrently against shared staging state that a locally warm, single-threaded run doesn't stress the same way. Fix: provision isolated data per test or per parallel worker via API calls.

flashcards.q: Why shouldn't visual regression testing and functional E2E testing be conflated in one suite/report?
flashcards.a: They test different bug classes -- a checkout flow can visually shift color and still functionally work, or look pixel-identical while functionally broken. Conflating them muddies what a red result actually means and slows triage, since each usually needs a different reviewer (design/product vs. engineering).

flashcards.q: What debugging tool reduces E2E triage time the most, versus a bare stack trace?
flashcards.a: Trace/video capture on failure (e.g., Playwright's trace viewer, which records DOM snapshots, network activity, and console output on a full timeline) -- it's the single biggest reducer of E2E debugging time compared to a bare stack trace.

flashcards.q: What is the E2E 'rot loop' and where does it start?
flashcards.a: Shared test data causes one test's side effect to break another -> flaky failure -> team reruns until green or merges on red -> suite grows with more journeys 'just in case' -> more flakiness surface -> loop compounds. It starts with unisolated test data, not with the tooling.
